title: Fame forgets
hook: everyone who remembers you will soon die too (Meditations 4.19)

segments.voice: Yesterday: time gained. Your line was run straight along the line, without swerving. Which comparison did you skip, and where did those minutes go instead? Day five hundred fifty-six.
screen: `RUN STRAIGHT ALONG THE LINE, WITHOUT SWERVING.`

segments.voice: Name your great-grandparents. All eight of them. Try it, without looking anything up. These were people who worked, loved, worried about money, told jokes at dinner, and were, for a while, the center of somebody's world. Three generations on, some of their names have slipped even from their own family. Marcus Aurelius, a man whose face was stamped on coins across an empire, did that same arithmetic about himself. And he used it to loosen the grip of wanting to be remembered. Today: fame forgets.
screen: `NAME ALL EIGHT GREAT-GRANDPARENTS.` → `THREE GENERATIONS LATER.` → `FAME FORGETS.`

segments.voice: First, the chain of the forgetting. In the nineteenth entry of book four Marcus writes about the person who longs to be remembered after death. They don't stop to think, he says, that every one of those who remember them will soon die too, and then those who come after, until the whole memory goes out, passed from one person to the next, through people who admire and then die. Second, suppose they don't die. Then Marcus pushes further. Suppose the people who remember you were immortal, and the memory too. What would that be to you? You'd be gone. Praise can't reach the dead. Third, even praise now. And to the living, he asks, what is praise, except for some practical use? It's information at best. It doesn't make the act better or worse. Fourth, no credit. So what's left is the act itself. If you do good to be remembered, you're building on something that will dissolve. If you do it because it's good, it's complete the moment it's done. This can sound bleak. But look at the questions it answers: will anyone notice, will this count, will they know it was me? Marcus sets them down. In the end, nobody will remember. So the good thing can be done without an audience, the way a great-grandmother might once have fed a neighbor's child and never written it down. Her name may be gone. The meal was still eaten.
screen: `EVERYONE WHO REMEMBERS WILL DIE TOO.` · `EVEN IF THEY DIDN'T, WHAT IS IT TO YOU?` · `PRAISE DOESN'T CHANGE THE ACT.` · `THE ACT IS COMPLETE WHEN DONE.` · then, large: `NO CREDIT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one person in your family line whose name you don't know, someone two or three generations back. Picture them at the end of an ordinary day, having done some small good nobody wrote down. Let them be uncredited and complete. Then choose one thing you could do today for no credit: something nobody will thank you for, or know was you. The bell holds the time.
Fame forgets. Marcus notes that everyone who remembers you will die too; so do good for its own sake, complete without credit. Today's word.
Your line: no credit. Do one good thing today that nobody will know was you. Day five hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes answer Meditations 4.19 with anonymous acts: a good deed done so that no one will know who did it.

original.note: Greek, 'after-fame', fame after death: the craving Marcus answers in 4.19. The same word ends book two: after-fame is oblivion.

trapdoor: what you thought: fame doesn't last.
what it means: since memory fades, do good for its own sake, complete without anyone's credit.
what a scholar hears: Marcus's word here is husterophemia, 'after-fame', the same word he set beside oblivion at the end of book two (2.17).

notes: 4.19 paraphrased: he who has a vehement desire for posthumous fame does not consider that every one who remembers him will himself also die very soon, then those who succeed them, until the whole remembrance is extinguished as it is transmitted through men who foolishly admire and perish; suppose those who remember were immortal, what is it to you? And to the living, what is praise, except for some utility? Confirm.
The Greek for posthumous fame in 4.19 is often given as husterophemia; the trapdoor paraphrases it as 'after-fame'. Confirm. The original game uses the common word doxa.
Marcus's portrait on coinage across the empire: standard; confirm wording.
